_comment: Catalogue for the practical-examples gallery at opentechevents.org/examples/. This file holds the STRUCTURE (which documents, in what order, under which filters, which fields to link) plus the English prose. Translations live next to it as <lang>.json and carry prose only. The code shown on the site is read from the documents themselves — never written here. CI fails if a document is missing from this file, if this file names a document that does not exist, or if a translation is missing: `npm run build-examples -- --check`.

examples.title: The smallest valid event
examples.summary: Six lines. This is the whole barrier to entry for a small meetup — everything else is optional.
points: Only `id`, `name`, `startDate` and `timezone` are required — plus `specVersion` and `license`, which a standalone document cannot inherit from a feed.

`url` and `description` are strongly recommended and still not required: most published .ics files carry neither, and a spec that demanded them would force importers to drop the event or invent the data.
`startDate` carries the time on the poster, with no UTC offset. `timezone` is what turns it into an unambiguous instant.

examples.title: Hybrid meetup, with everything you'd normally want
examples.summary: A venue and a joining URL at once, topics, coordinates, a poster, a free ticket — and one field that is not part of the spec yet.
points: `location` and `attendanceMode` answer different questions: `location` is observable fact (is there a venue? is there a URL?), `attendanceMode` is the organiser's intent. If they disagree, `attendanceMode` wins.

`venue` and `address` are the same place said twice on purpose: `venue` is the one string iCal and RSS can print, `address` is the five parts a schema.org `PostalAddress` needs — and Google validates them one by one.
`updatedAt` is what lets a consumer sync incrementally — it is iCal's `LAST-MODIFIED`, not `DTSTAMP`.
`image` lists the SAME poster in three crops, most useful first: several sizes of one image, not a gallery. Only the first survives iCal.
`offers` with a single `price: 0` is how a free event says so. Leaving `offers` out does NOT mean free — it means the price is unknown, which is a different claim.

`capacity` is NOT in v0.4. The document is valid anyway: the schemas do not forbid extra fields, on purpose. That is how the spec grows — through fields someone already uses, which is exactly how `image` and `offers` got in.

examples.title: A monthly meetup: one document per occurrence
examples.summary: This is June's edition, not the series. OTE never puts a recurrence rule in the feed — whoever publishes expands it.
points: One document = one occurrence. Twelve editions are twelve documents, each with its own `id`, dates and `status`. `partOf` only says which set they belong to.
That is what makes cancelling August possible: `status: "cancelled"` on that occurrence's own document, which stays published so subscribers find out.
A consumer that ignores `partOf` still sees a complete, correct event. A recurrence rule it ignored would leave it with no dates at all.
`ics:rrule` is someone else's vocabulary — the prefix says so. The importer keeps it for lossless round-trips; nobody is required to expand it.

examples.title: Online-only session, in two languages, behind a community door
examples.summary: No venue, just a joining URL — a weekly series behind it, a membership in front of it, and a text that exists in Catalan and Spanish.
points: `location` carries `onlineUrl` and nothing else. An empty `location: {}` is invalid: saying nothing is already done by omitting the field.

`eligibility` is the third part of "can I go?": `attendanceMode` and `location` say the event is within reach of anyone with a connection, this says there is still a door — the voice channel lives inside the community's Discord. Its `url` is where the condition is met, not where a seat is bought: that is `offers[].url`.

`languages` and `textLanguage` are not the same data, and here they disagree: Catalan and Spanish are SPOKEN at the session, and the document is WRITTEN in Catalan only. Neither derives from the other, and both use BCP 47 tags.

`translations` carries the Spanish version of `name` and `description` — while those two fields stay plain strings, so a v0.2 consumer reads this document without noticing the field exists. There is no `ca` entry: that would be the same text twice.

Text that lives INSIDE an object is translated where it lives: `eligibility.translations` and `partOf.translations`, never a positional mirror like `translations.es.partOf.name`. `location.venue` and `organizers[].name` are never translated at all — they are proper nouns.
Weekly sessions are published the same way monthly ones are: one document per session, grouped by `partOf`.

examples.title: A hackathon that runs through the night
examples.summary: Starts Saturday morning, ends Sunday evening, never stops. One event — and deliberately no `partOf`.
points: A continuous event crossing midnight is exactly what `startDate`/`endDate` are for: both date-times, both in the same form.
Compare with the multi-part study jam below. There the dates are NOT continuous, which is why it becomes several documents instead of one.
Two organisers — the community and its host venue. Order matters: the first is the principal one, and the only one that survives translation to iCal.

examples.title: One study jam, three non-consecutive Saturdays
examples.summary: The case that tempts everyone into stretching the dates. Three documents, one `partOf` with `type: "multipart"`.
points: Do NOT write `startDate` on the first Saturday and `endDate` on the last: that claims a continuous fifteen-day event and blocks two full weeks in every subscriber's calendar.
`type: "multipart"` is not decoration — it changes the translation. A series becomes schema.org `EventSeries`; a multi-part event becomes an `Event` whose parts are its `subEvent`.
What `multipart` does not model is "one single registration". That is not a date — it is ticketing, which v0.4 leaves out. Don't fix it by deforming the time fields.

examples.title: A two-day conference, all-day form
examples.summary: Dates without times, when the schedule isn't the point yet.
points: Both dates use the same form. Mixing (a date for `startDate`, a date-time for `endDate`) is rejected by the schema.
For all-day events `timezone` contextualises the date — it says which region that day belongs to. It does not shift it, and a consumer must not convert it to another zone.

`endDate: "2026-10-17"` is inclusive — the event runs through the 17th, which is why this is two days, not one. Exported to iCalendar that's `DTEND;VALUE=DATE:20261018` (one day later): RFC 5545 defines DTEND as the non-inclusive end, the opposite convention.

examples.title: A URL with a Spanish slug
examples.summary: The address people publish and share contains `ñ`, and the document keeps that spelling.
points: `id` and `url` accept HTTP(S) IRIs, not only ASCII URIs. A browser-valid slug like `pycamp-españa` is valid OTE.
The identifier is compared byte-for-byte by consumers, so a publisher must mint it once and keep the same spelling instead of switching later to a percent-encoded form.
The same rule applies to image URLs: the schema still requires an absolute HTTP(S) IRI, but it no longer rejects a real image path because the scheme is `http` or the filename is not ASCII.

examples.title: Conference with tickets and an open call for papers
examples.summary: Three ticket tiers and a call for proposals — the two things people search a conference for, and neither of them was in v0.2.
points: Tiered pricing is several `offers`, not one with a range: a price you cannot write as a single number is more than one offer. `availability` says which tier is already gone.
The student tier is `price: 0` and no `currency` — free is free in every currency, and asking for one there is how a free meetup ends up publishing a US dollar amount.
The deadlines carry an offset, unlike the event's own dates. A CFP closing at "23:59" is the classic bug: which midnight is the entire question, and "anywhere on Earth" is a real answer (`-12:00`).

The free student places ran out and a queue opened: `sold-out` + `waitlistUrl`, not a third `availability` value. Every consumer that already exists keeps reading "sold out" — which is true, you cannot buy — while one that knows the field offers the queue. `price: 0` next to `sold-out` is not a contradiction: `price` describes the deal, `availability` whether you can act on it now.

`offers[].name` is free text on purpose — an enum would take away an organiser's right to name their own tickets — so translating it is the price, and it is done INSIDE the offer. The rest of the offer has no language at all: `price` is a number, `currency` a code, `availability` an enum.

`cfp` has no equivalent in schema.org, iCal or RSS — it degrades to text on export. It is in the core anyway because "which conferences are accepting proposals right now" is a question only the publisher can answer, and today it is answered by scraping.

examples.title: Three organisers, and another project's vocabulary
examples.summary: Two communities and a person — plus a prefixed field that belongs to a community directory, not to OTE.
points: `organizers` is a list because co-organisation is the norm, not the exception. Order is significant: the first one is the principal.
`type` defaults to `organization`: a translator has to pick a schema.org `@type` either way, and `Organization` is the tolerant choice.
`combuilders:communityId` is not an OTE field. OTE promises never to mint a field name containing a colon, so prefixed fields cannot collide with the core — today or at 1.0.

examples.title: Imported from an .ics file
examples.summary: What an importer can honestly produce from a calendar file — including what it must leave out.
points: No `attendanceMode`, because iCalendar cannot express it. Staying silent and saying `in-person` are different claims, and only one is honest.

`location.address` is missing, and the checker says so — an `.ics` carries `LOCATION` as one free-text line, with no parts to split it into. The warning names what the event lacks, not who is to blame for it.
`source` is required when the event was imported or aggregated. It is orthogonal to `organizers`: who runs the event vs. where the data came from.
`source.license` (what the origin allows) and `license` (what this document allows) are different fields. Declaring a licence does not grant rights the origin never gave.

examples.title: A community feed, and how inheritance works
examples.summary: `license` and `organizers` sit on the feed and flow down. One event overrides them — and that override replaces, it does not merge.
points: Repeating `"license": "CC-BY-4.0"` in 200 events is noise, not rigour: an event that omits it inherits the feed's.
An event that declares `organizers` REPLACES the inherited list. With merging there would be no way to remove an inherited organiser.
That is why the second event repeats the feed's own community next to the guest one: leaving it out would attribute the event to the guest alone.

`textLanguage` inherits the same way: declared once on the feed, no event repeats it. That is what makes the field cost one line for a monolingual publisher. `translations` never inherits — it translates the FEED's title, not its events' names.

examples.title: An aggregator feed
examples.summary: Someone publishing events they do not organise — the case where getting `organizers` wrong misattributes everything.
points: An aggregator feed must OMIT `organizers`: it does not run what it publishes, so every event states its own.
`feed.title`/`url` name whoever publishes the feed. Never fall back to them for attribution — that is exactly how an aggregator ends up credited for every event it aggregates.
The cancelled event stays in the feed. Deleting it silently leaves a dead event in subscribers' calendars with no way to find out.

examples.title: Who is on stage
examples.summary: A panel: three speakers on one talk, each with a canonical page and their other profiles.
points: `speakers` is not `organizers`: whoever gives the talk did not organise it. Putting a speaker in `organizers` corrupts the data for everyone who consumes it.
It is a list because a panel is the norm. `type` defaults to `person` — the opposite of `organizers` — because a speaker is overwhelmingly a person.
`url` is one canonical page; `sameAs` is the list of other profiles, mapping to schema.org `Person.sameAs`. `speakers` is deliberately NOT in the recommended profile: an `.ics` importer never has it.

examples.title: Where the data came from, and where to fix it
examples.summary: An aggregated event carries `source` (provenance) and `contributing` (a correction channel) — different fields, both present.
points: `source.url` points UPSTREAM, at the record the data came from. Correcting it there does not fix a mapping bug the aggregator introduced.
`contributing` points at where THIS record is fixed. It exists because an aggregator must leave `organizers` out, so the field that could carry a contact is gone.
`contributing` is inherited from `feed.contributing` like `license`; a declared value replaces the inherited one.

examples.title: A JSON-only feed that points at its other formats
examples.summary: No HTML page in front of it, so `alternates` is the only place to say the same collection is also RSS and iCal.
points: `alternates` is the JSON form of an HTML `<link rel="alternate">`, for feeds served as a bare endpoint.
It is INFORMATIONAL: a consumer must not assume the linked RSS/iCal is in sync with this feed; a producer should generate them from the same source.
`feed.contributing` here is a `mailto:` role address — the form dev.events uses for corrections.

examples.title: Linking the recording after the fact
examples.summary: The event is over; the recording is added to the same record, same id, new updatedAt.
points: `recordings` is not `image` (the poster) and not `location.onlineUrl` (the live link, which stops meaning the same thing once the event ends).
A list: the talk is on YouTube and the Q&A on the community's own PeerTube. The second entry has a `title` because there is more than one.
`recordings` is NOT recommended: most events have no recording, a live one has none yet, and the spec has no 'is in the past' predicate.

examples.title: A conference ticket, and a workshop on top
examples.summary: A paid workshop that is a PART of a conference: partOf.offers carries the shared admission, the workshop's own offer is an add-on.
points: `partOf.offers` is the shared admission — the conference ticket — written identically on every part, so a consumer holding one part can price it without resolving the parent.
`scope: "add-on"` means this offer is ON TOP of the admission: total = 240 (admission) + 60 (add-on). An `add-on` offer requires `partOf.offers` in the same document.
Tier-specific coverage (a workshop only for Full tickets), per-day passes, bundles and coupons are out of scope for v0.5 — see DECISIONS.md.

examples.title: Both parts of a paid multi-part event
examples.summary: Two documents sharing one partOf.id, both carrying the same partOf.offers block — which the validator enforces.
points: The keynote has no `offers` of its own: it is COVERED by `partOf.offers`. That is the one place an absent `offers` list means something other than unknown.
The workshop repeats the SAME `partOf.offers` block, byte for byte in meaning — `sharedOffersConsistent` rejects a feed where two parts of one set disagree.
This relaxes the 'a consumer that ignores partOf still sees correct events' guarantee for PRICING only: ignoring `partOf.offers` yields incomplete pricing, never wrong pricing.

examples.title: A two-day conference with parallel tracks
examples.summary: Five sessions over two days, two rooms running at once — each its own document, all sharing one partOf.
points: Parallel tracks need no new field: two sessions at the same time are two documents with overlapping dates and a different location.venue (Sala A / Sala B). One document = one occurrence.
Every session carries the SAME partOf.offers block — the conference admission — written identically. sharedOffersConsistent rejects a feed where two parts of one set disagree.
Most sessions have no offers of their own: they are covered by partOf.offers. The Pact workshop has scope: "add-on" — total to attend it is the admission plus 45.
The opening keynote is plenary (no parallel track); the rest pair up. Each session lists its speakers.
